Fresh Tenders for Haj Flights 
* 121.   SHRIMATI JAYAPRADA NAHATA: † 
SHRI AMAR SINGH: 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to stale: 
(a) whether Government had invited fresh tenders for engagement of aircrafts
for Haj Flights despite the fact that the company entrusted with this exercise was 
ioing good job and if so, the reasons therefor; 
(b) the details of rates quoted by each company alongwith the term s and
onditions; and

THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) to (c) 
Global tenders are invited every year for wetlease of aircrafts for Haj Operations. 
"harter company for Haj operations is  selected through global tendering 
rocedure and not on the basis of only past performance of charter company ho 
had undertaken the previous Haj operations. However, the company, which 
onducted the Haj 2000 operations, has been black listed on account of its poor 
jerformance. The selection of charter company for Haj-2001 is yet to be finalised.

Minister has focussed on the performances. But my question is this. The Indian 
Government had invited tenders for Haj flights. Air India charges Rs. 31,200/-
towards Haj fare. Out of this, the Haj pilgrim is paying Rs. 12,600/- and the 
Government is paying Rs. 18,600/-. It is a good thing. But I think, the other 
Airlines are charging between Rs. 21,000 and Rs. 24,000. Mr. Chairman, Sir, I 
would like to know what is the minimum fare? Why is the Air India not able to do 
it? If it was there, what was the reason for not awarding the contract to the 
°ompany which quoted the lowest tender in this regard.

Projects 
*126. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO:  Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have constituted a High-Level Committee for early 
clearance and implementation of Ichampalli and Polavaram Projects for 
utilisation of Godavari Waters; 
(b) if so, the composition of the Committee; and 
(c) by when the Committee would submit its report? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN SETHI): (a) 
to (c) A High Level Committee has been constituted on the 6th July, 2000 
under the Chairmanship of Member, Water Planning & Projects (WP&P), 
Central Water Commission (CWC) with representatives from Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Orissa as Member, Chief Engineer (Project 
Appraisal), CWC as Member, Chief Engineer (Irrigation Management) CWC, as 
Member Secretary and representatives from the Central Electricity Authority,

Central Ground Water Board, National Water Development Agency, Ministry of 
Environment and Forests as invitee Members to resolve the inter- State issues 
involved in Ichampalti and Polavaram Projects. The Committee is likely to submit 
its report by January, 2001. 
SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Sir, the Ichampalli and Polavaram projects have 
been pending for the last 22 years. What concrete steps have been taken by the 
Government to ensure their implementation? Despite the neighbouring States 
accepting the Bachawat Committee recommendations, I would like to know why

metres to 38.10 metres in the case of  Polavaram project, as against the 
recommendations of the Bachawat Committee. As the height proposed by the 
Central Water Commission would not help in supplying water to the agricultural land 
in Telangana, will the Government reconsider increasing the height of the projects, as 
recommended by the Bachawat Committee? 
SHRI ARJUN SETHI: Mr. Chairman, Sir, these two projects are inter-State 
projects. The States of Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh now Chhattisgarh and 
Orissa are involved in the Polavaram project; and the States of Maharashtra and 
Andhra Pradesh and the erstwhile State of Madhya Pradesh are involved in the 
Ichampalli project. These are inter-State projects and, therefore, all the parties have 
to agree for the implementation of these two projects. If these States are agreeable 
and have a consensus on the issues involved, the Centre can do something. The 
Centre cannot, on its own, impose something on these States. At the request of the 
hon. Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, a committee has been constituted. As I have 
already answered in the main reply, a committee has been constituted and the first 
meeting has already taken place. As I have stated in the main reply, the committee 
is likely to submit its report on the implementation of these projects, by January, 
2001.

were planned to benefit 1.576 and 7.19 lakh acres of land, besides 975 and 720

STs and OBCs. In the above circumstances, I would like to request the 
Government to take up these projects as national projects.

RBI have issued guidelines to public sector banks dated July 27/28, 2000 
24 

[28 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
prescribing a simplified, non-discriminatory and non-discretionary mechanism for 
recovery of the stock of NPAs of banks and financial institutions in all sectors. 
The guidelines are in two parts, Part-A and Part-B. Part-A contains detailed 
guidelines for recovery of NPAs upto Rs. 5.00 crore. Part-B contains guidelines for 
recovery of NPAs over Rs. 5.00 crore, the details of which are as follows:— 
(i) CMDs should personally supervise the NPAs of Rs. 5.00 crore and above
on case to case basis. A list of such NPAs should be prepared and all cases
reviewed by CMD personally and the course of action decided in terms of 
rehabilitation/restructuring, one time settlement or filing of suits. 
(ii) The Board of Directors may evolve policy guidelines regarding one time
settlement of NPAs over Rs. 5.00 crore covering the computation formula,
realisable amount, cut off date and payment conditions with reference to
factors of security and disposability, etc.
(iii) In respect of defaulters, who have not come up for one time settlement by
given time, or where restructuring is not feasible, suits must be filed in
all such cases. Banks should follow up suit filed cases vigorously and
effectively in the Courts to enable DRTs to decide the cases within 6
months as laid down in the DRT Act and realisation of dues completed at the
earliest.
The guidelines do not, apply to cases of wilful default, fraud and malfeasance 
where in each case banks have been asked to initiate prompt action for 
realisation. 
(c) The guidelines issued in July 2000 for NPAs below Rs. 5 crore envisage a
simplified, non- discretionary and non-discriminatory mechanism for recovery of the 
stock of NPAs. The banks have to identify NPAs in the doubtful or loss category as 
on 31st March, 1997 and give notice to the eligible defaulting borrowers to avail of

THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS (SHRI RAM VILAS 
PASWAN): (a) to (d) The Government had appointed a consortium of 
Consultants led by M/s A.F. Ferguson & Co. to assist in the development and

Telecom Services (DTS)/Department of Telecom Operations (DTO). Keeping

Reduction in the Cost of Rural Telephones 
* 140. SHRI R. S. GAVAI; Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have decided and selected technologies to be used for 
providing rural telephones; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether any Committee has been set-up for this purpose; 
(d) if so, the details of the recommendations made by the Committee; 
and

THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS (SHRI RAM VILAS 
PASWAN): (a) to (e) An empowered Committee was set up under the 
chairmanship of Minister of State for Communications to examine and suggest 
suitable technologies for rural development. The Committee recommended diree 
technologies, viz. Wireless in Local Loop (WLL), Time Division Multiple 
Access/Point to Multi Point (C-DOT TD MA/PMP) and Satellite. In addition, 
landlines/cables should continue to be adopted for providing VPTs. While 
accepting the recommendations of the Empowered Committee, the 
Government has also planned to set up Small and Medium capacity exchanges to 
provide telephone connections in rural areas. These exchanges are state-of-the-art 
Digital Electronics Exchanges based on C-DOT design. Transmission media of 
adequate capacity will also be installed to provide reliable connectivity to the 
exchanges working in rural areas. 
GSM system is also proposed to be inducted in the network. Depending 
upon coverage, GSM system will also provide telephones in the rural areas. 
Wireless technologies are proving more cost effective for providing 
telephones to subscribers far away from telephone exchanges in comparison 
to underground cables. Induction of the above technologies based on wireless 
options will be cost effective depending upon the terrain and the topography of 
the area.

Memorandum by United Forum of Bank Unions 
882. SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE: Will th e Minister of FINANC E
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a memorandum has been presented by the United Forum  of
Bank Unions to the Prime Minister on 28th October, 2000 regarding the 
proposed move of Government to reduce Government equity in Nationalised 
Banks; 
(b) if so, the salient content of the same; and
(c) the action taken by Government in this regard?
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHR I
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The salient feature of the Memorandum are as under:—
1. Reducing Government equity in nationalised banks from 51%
to 33% is against the interests of the nation, national economy, banking 
industry and bank employees. 
2. Privatisation of banks is aimed at diverting people's attentio n
from ever increasing portfolios of bad and doubtful debts (non 
performing assets). 
3. Public sector character of nationalised banks be maintained.
4. Privatisation of banks will effect priority sector lending.
(c) It is proposed to amend the Banking Companies (Acquisition and
Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970/1980 with a view to modifying the 
stipulation of minimum prescribed Government shareholding in nationalised 
banks from 51% to 33%. Necessary legisl ation in this regard is likely to be 
introduced in the current session of th e Parliament. As announced by Finance 
Minister in his budget speech for 2000-2001 in view of budgetary constraints 
with regard to further recapitalisation of nationalised banks, the amendment 
is being made to enable banks to raise capital from the market as and when 
required in future in order to meet th e capital adequacy norms prescribed by 
Reserve Bank of India. The public sect or character of banks will however be 
maintained. The Government has no proposal to disinvest its equity in 
nationalised banks.

Distribution of Water Resources 
972. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY:  Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the main objectives and salient features of the National Water Policy 
framed in 1987; 
(b) whether the aforesaid objectives have been fulfilled; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) what steps are proposed to be taken to ensure a fair and equitable 
181 

RAJYA SABHA [ 28 November, 2000] 
distribution of the existing water resources available in the country amongst 
the various States through a process of concilliation and consensus? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES 
(SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) The main objectives of the National 
Water Policy adopted in 1987 are that planning and development of water 
resources should be governed by National Perspectives and the drainage basin 
should be considered as the basic unit of planning for development of water 
resources and their optimum utilization. The Salient features of the policy are 
given in the Statement (See below). 
(b) and (c) Water being a State subject necessary follow up actions on the 
National Water Policy (NWP) are being taken by the States. State Water Policy 
has been framed by Government of Kerala, Orissa, Tamil Nadu and Uttar 
Pradesh. Central Government gives nece ssary assistance to states by way of 
technical guidance and financial support in this endeavour. 
(d) The Inter State issues are resolved through mutual discussions amongst 
the states and over 130 inter state agre ements have been arrived at between 
states so far. Issues not settled through negotiations are referred to inter state 
water dispute tribunal which can be constituted under the Inter State Water 
Disputes (ISWD) Act. 1956. Amendments to the Act are proposed, on the 
recommendations of the Sarkaria Commission, agreed to by the Inter-State 
Council, the draft Policy Guidelines for Allocation of Water amongst the 
State prepared by the National Water Board to ensure fair and equitable 
distribution of the existing water resources has been referred to the Working 
Group of Ministers of all States/Union Territories constituted under the 
Chairmanship of Union Minister of Water Resources to achieve greater 
convergence and agreement on issues involving divergent views by the 
National Water Resources Council. 
Statement 
The Salient Features of the NWP 1987 
—  Water is a precious national resource and its development   should 
be governed by national perspectives; 
—  The available resources, both surface and groundwater, should be 
made utilizable to the maximum extent; 
—  Planning for water resources to be on the basis of the hydrological 
182 

[28 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
unit such as a drainage basin or sub-basin. Appropriate 
organizations should be established for the planned development 
and management of the river basins as a whole; 
—  Water should be made available to areas where there is a shortage by 
transfer from other areas including transfer from one river basin lo 
another, after taking into account the requirements ofihe basins; 
—  Project planning for development of water resources should, as far 
as possible, be for multiple benefits based on integrated and multi-
disciplinary approach having regard to human and ecological aspects 
and special needs of disadvantaged sections of the society. 
—  In the allocation of water ordinarily first priority should be for drinking 
water, with irrigation, hydro-power, industrial and other uses following 
in that order; 
—  The groundwater potential should be periodically reassessed and its 
exploitation regulated with refere nce to recharge possibilities and 
consideration of social equity; 
—  Due care should be taken right from the project planning stage lo 
promote conjunctive use of surface and groundwater; 
—  Maintenance, modernization and safety of structures should be 
ensured through proper organizational arrangements: 
—  There should be close integration of water use and land use policies 
and distribution of water should be with due regard to equity a«v! 
social justice; 
—  E f f ic iency of ut i I i za I i o n should be i m pro v ed i n  all the d iversion of water 
and conservation consciousness promoted through edi... urn MI. 
regulation, incentives and disincentives; 
—  Water rates should be such as to foster the motivation lor economy 
in water use and should adequately co\er lhe annual maintenance 
and operational charges and a part of the fixed cost. 
—  Farmers should be progressively invoked in the management of 
irrigation system; 
—  There should be a Master Plan for flood control mid management 
for each flood prone basin. In flood control and management, the 
strategy should be to reduce the intensity of floods by sound 
watershed management and provision of adequate flood cushion in 
water storage projects wherever f easible to facilitate belter flood 
management of each flood prone basin; 
183 

RAJYA SABHA (28 November, 2000] 
—  Land erosion by sea or river should be minimized by suitable cost-
effective measures. Indiscriminate occupation of, and economic 
activity in coastal areas and flood plain zones should be regulated; 
—  Needs of drought-prone areas should be given priority in the planning 
of project for development of water resources. These areas should 
be made less vulnerable through soil moisture conservation 
measures, water harvesting practices, the minimization of evaporation 
losses, the development of ground water potential and transfer of 
surface water from surplus areas wh ere feasible and appropriate. 
Pastures, forestry or other modes of development which are relatively 
less water demanding should be encouraged. 
—  A national information system on water resources should be 
established with a net-work of data banks and data bases integrating 
and strengthening the existing Central and Stale level agencies; 
—  Training and research efforts should be intensified as an integral 
part of water resources development programmers.

SHRI NILOTPAL BASU (West B engal): Mr. Chairman. Sir, 
before he starts, I would like to take your permission for speaking for 
only two minutes on a very serious issue. Today, throughout the 
country — and in Delhi also - lakhs of bank employees are raising 
their voice against the obnoxious attempt by the Government of India 
to denationalise the djfferent national ised banks that we have in the 
country. We know that the banki ng system was in the doldrums when 
it was under the private sector. Once  it was nationalised, it paved the 
way for developmental banking and huge resources were available 
with the Government. The public sector banks have played a big role 
In the development of the country,  in the development of the social 
sector and in the development of the infrastructure. Now, we have 
seen that in the post-nationalisation period, some \7 private banks 
which had failed were taken over by the Government; and they have 
been functioning in a proper manner. Now, Rs.1,00,000 crore of bad 
money is there in the banking system which we euphemistically call 
"the non-performing assets (NPA)*. Instead of recovering this huge 
amount, together with the interest,   the Government is

they should be denationalised. Over and above that, they are indulging 
in this hypocracy by bringing down the stakes of the Government to 
below 50 per cent and still saying th at they would allow the banks to 
continue with their public sector character. It is a btatant falsehood 
because there will be teji non-offici af private sector  directors in a

banks. As I said, about Rs.l,00,000 crores of bad money is there. They 
should try to recover this amount, instead of resorting to

Yesterday, we started a Short Duration Discussion on the 
plight of farmers in the country, The Leader of the Opposition, Dr. 
Manmohan Singh, also recommended more public sector investment 
for the development of our agriculture which is languishing. This is a 
question which is agitating the eirtire country. In this situation, we are 
finding that the Government is going in for this ominous attempt to 
denationalise the nationalised banks and give a fillip to all those 
people who have defaulted on the repay ment of their loans to the 
banks. 
Therefore, I want the entire House to join me in demanding of 
the Government that they would not go ahead with denationalisation 
of the different public sector banks. Thank you.

SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN (Kerala): Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, the peasants and agricultural workers in our country are 
experiencing extreme difficulties and hardships. Never before in the 
history of Independent India, peasants and agricultural labourers faced 
so serious a threat to their liveli hood as it is now. Certain policies 
pursued by the Government in the name of reform programmes have 
aggravated the crisis. If this crisis prolongs, it may develop into a 
severe crisis engulfing all the sectors of economy.   So, it is necessary 
to take practical measures to solve this crisis. 
Peasants and agricultural workers are very restive and have 
begun to resort to various forms of  struggle. Tens of thousands of 
peasants and agricultural workers belonging to different political 
shades and different States will come over to the capital city of Delhi 
on 30th of this month to demonstrate before Parliament to press their 
demands, 
Lifting Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) on imports is one such 
step which had worked havoc. It is said to have been done to comply 
with the WTO agreement. But, in fact, the quantitative restrictions have 
been withdrawn before the time-limit stipulated in the WTO agreement. 
The European Union, and several countries like Britain, Japan, 
Canada and Australia had agreed that the quantitative restrictions may 
be withdrawn only by March 31 s', 2003, But, the USA alone 
pressurised India to do it earlier, and the Government of India 
succumbed to this pressure and agree d to lift quantitative restrictions 
on 715 items on March 31 st, 2000; and the balance on 31 s1 March, 
2001. Maybe, it was done to win the favour of the USA. But this is 
done at the expense of the peasants, agricultural labourers and the 
national interests. The prices of most of the agricultural crops have 
fallen heavily. I may state a few cases. Prices of coc onut fell from Rs. 7 
to 8 to Rs. 2 per nut; price of rubber fell from Rs. 60-65 per kg to Rs. 25-30; 
price   of   coffee from Rs. 58 to Rs. 30; and price of tea

from Rs. 15 to Rs. 3. Due to heavy fall in prices, the peasants have 
incurred heavy losses. Their indebtedness has increased. Marginal 
and poor peasants are those who suffered the most. In fact, the 
peasants are in great distress and the desperation is leading them to 
take extreme steps like suicides. In the case of agricultural labourers, 
their working days in a year have further declined. Their real wages 
have also gone down. The refusal of the Government to pass a 
comprehensive legislation for the ben efit of the agricultural workers 
has made their situation worse. Now, I would like to appeal to the 
Government, through you, Madam Chairperson, to take urgent steps to 
introduce and pass such a Bill. 
The steps taken by the Government to ensure a minimum 
support price (MSP) have failed miserably. In several cases, the 
peasants had to sell their product s at prices less than the MSP 
declared. This system will have to  be reviewed and improved upon to 
ensure the peasants the MSP. Another  step taken by the Government 
is to cut down subsidies. The Government has increased the price of 
fertilizers, pesticides, ch arges on electricity, i rrigation water, etc. The 
price of diesel has been increased by 60 per cent. This has added to 
the worries of the peasants, This is also being done in the name of 
complying with the terms of the WTO Agreement. But, strangely 
enough, the highly developed countries like the USA, EU and Japan 
are giving high subsidies to their farmers. They are also given higher 
export subsidies. The subsidies that are paid to the farmers in India 
are very much less. Yet, the developed countries are compelling India 
to cut subsidies, and, strangely enoug h, the Government of India is 
yielding to their pressure and has declared that subsidies would be 
fuily abolished shortly. 
The devastating floods and drought which affected various 
States and vast areas have confounded the situation. The Government 
has failed to take effective relief measures. In the cf:se of West 
Bengal, it pursued a policy of discrimination. Increasing the prices of 
foodgrains distributed through the Publ ic Distribution System had led 
to a virtual dismantling of the Public Distribution System. This has le.j 
to a serious situation on the foodg rains front. The offtake from the 
PiDS has been drastically reduced. The Food Corporation of India 
godowns are full with foodgrains. Further procurement has become 
difficult and the peasants had to undersell their produce. This has also 
added to the crista.   Thus,  a very serious crisis has

developed in the agrarian sector.   If this crisis prolongs, it may 
develop into a severe economic crisis,   embracing all sectors of the 
economy. 
The National Agricultural Policy which was announced will not 
help in improving the situation. Its proposes reversal of the existing 
ceiling laws and would lead to dispossession of peasants of their 
lands. It will also clear the path for the entry of multinationals in the 
agricultural sector. Therefore, I appeal to the Government through you, 
Madam Deputy Chairperson, to review the entire policies and adopt 
concrete practical measures to find a solution to the crisis, Thank you.

Vice-Chairman, Sir, today we are discussing a very vital issue. 
Agriculture is the backbone of our country. Sir, 70 per cent of our

only self-sufficient in foodgrains, but we have also become an 
exporting country. In many parts of the country our farmers are 
suffering from  drought and floods.

Government's policies. Sir, I am emphasising on Andhra Pradesh not 
only because I belong to that State but also because we are based on 
agriculture; Andhra Pradesh is an agri cultural State. Our farmers are 
frequently suffering, as I said, because of calamities created by floods 
as well as droughts every year, Our hon. Chief Minister has taken 
enough precautions, but in spite of taking all actions, the farmers are 
suffering. There is no change in the plight of the farmers. Also, 
because of the strict norms adopted by the FCI this year, the paddy 
prices have dipped and the
